title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
Before you start
Five short steps, in your module-13-scales-facets project. Every output below comes from R 4.6.1.
1. Which R? Posit Cloud uses R 4.6.1. R 4.5 and later have their own penguins, with shorter column names (step 5).

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)"


2. Are the packages installed? TRUE means installed.

"palmerpenguins" %in% rownames(installed.packages())

[1] TRUE

"gapminder" %in% rownames(installed.packages())

[1] TRUE


3. Install only if step 2 said FALSE, once per project. (The same for palmerpenguins.)

install.packages("gapminder")

4. Load the packages every new session. You install a package once per project; you load it with library() each time R starts.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(gapminder)

5. Use the palmerpenguins version of penguins.

penguins <- palmerpenguins::penguins

names(palmerpenguins::penguins)

[1] "species"           "island"            "bill_length_mm"   
[4] "bill_depth_mm"     "flipper_length_mm" "body_mass_g"      
[7] "sex"               "year"             

names(datasets::penguins)

[1] "species"     "island"      "bill_len"    "bill_dep"    "flipper_len"
[6] "body_mass"   "sex"         "year"       


:: means “from this package”, as in scales::percent in Session 1. Here it makes sure we get the palmerpenguins version of penguins, not the one built into R.
Last, the course’s colors, once per session:

# Colors that color-blind viewers can tell apart
options(
  ggplot2.discrete.fill = function() scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8),
  ggplot2.discrete.colour = function() scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8)
)

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D1 · Label it
Prepares Guided Project task 1 (A1, B1).
Goal. A reader should understand the plot without you there: a title that says what it shows, a subtitle with the data and its n (sample size: the number of penguins in each group), axis titles with units, a legend title, and percent labels for a share. (Session 1.)
Your turn. Label the share of Adelie penguins on each island.

ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species == "Adelie")) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "___",
    subtitle = "___",
    x = "___",
    y = "___",
    fill = "___"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = ___)

Investigate. Which label would a reader miss most if you left it out?






TipSolution






ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species == "Adelie")) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Torgersen's penguins are all Adelie",
    subtitle = "Palmer penguins, 344 penguins on three islands",
    x = "Share of the island's penguins (%)",
    y = "Island",
    fill = "Adelie"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)








The title states the finding; the subtitle says which data and how many; the x-axis says “share of what” and its unit. Torgersen is 100% Adelie (52 of 52), Dream about 45% (56 of 124), Biscoe about 26% (44 of 168).

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D2 · Choose a scale
Prepares Guided Project task 2 (A2, B2).
Goal. Which scale fits the data? (Session 1.)
Your turn. Plot life expectancy against GDP per person in 2007, first on a linear x-axis, then on a log x-axis.

gap_2007 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007)

p_wealth <- ggplot(gap_2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")

p_wealth
p_wealth + ___(labels = scales::comma)

Investigate. Where are most countries on the linear axis? What does the log axis show that the linear one hides?






TipSolution





gap_2007 <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007)

p_wealth <- ggplot(gap_2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")

p_wealth
p_wealth +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)")










GDP per person runs from about $278 to $49,357 across 142 countries, and 66 of them are below $5,000: on a linear axis they crowd into the left edge. On a log axis each step is ten times the one before, so the poorer countries spread out and the pattern (life expectancy rises with each tenfold step) shows. Say “log scale” in the axis title: a reader who misses it reads the gaps wrong.

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D3 · The Lie Factor
Prepares Guided Project task 2: a scale is honest only if sizes in the picture match the data.
The Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) compares the size of an effect in the picture with its size in the data: drawn ratio ÷ data ratio. 1 is honest; above 1 exaggerates; below 1 understates.

lie_factors <- tibble(
  case = c("Module 12: penguin bars zoomed to start at 40",
           "Minard's march, default line widths (1 to 6)",
           "Minard's march, range = c(0.1, 8.5)"),
  drawn_ratio = c((168 - 40) / (52 - 40), 6 / 1, 8.5 / 0.1),
  data_ratio = c(168 / 52, 340000 / 4000, 340000 / 4000)
) %>%
  mutate(lie_factor = drawn_ratio / data_ratio)

lie_factors

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  case                                         drawn_ratio data_ratio lie_factor
  <chr>                                              <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Module 12: penguin bars zoomed to start at …        10.7       3.23     3.30  
2 Minard's march, default line widths (1 to 6)         6        85        0.0706
3 Minard's march, range = c(0.1, 8.5)                 85        85        1     


Talk. Which case exaggerates, which understates, and which is honest? Why does the default width scale understate Minard’s losses so much?






TipSolution






Bars cut at 40, about 3.3: exaggerates. Biscoe (168) looks about 10.7 times as long as Torgersen (52), but the counts differ only 3.2 times.
Minard, default widths, about 0.07: understates. The army shrinks from 340,000 to 4,000 (85 times), but scale_linewidth() draws widths from 1 to 6 by default: only 6 times. (In class you measured them with layer_data().)
Minard, range = c(0.1, 8.5), 1: honest. 8.5 ÷ 0.1 = 85, the same ratio as the data.

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D4 · Fixed or free panels
Prepares Guided Project task 3 (A3, B3).
Goal. One plot or many? And when the panels differ in size, fixed or free axes? (Session 2.)
Your turn. Plot each continent’s total population over time, one panel per continent. Then free the y-axis.

pop_by_continent <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarize(pop_millions = sum(pop) / 1e6, .groups = "drop")

p_pop <- ggplot(pop_by_continent, aes(x = year, y = pop_millions)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population (millions)")

p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(___))
p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(___), scales = "___")

Investigate. On the fixed panels, what happened to Oceania between 1952 and 2007? On the free panels? Which version would mislead a reader, and how?






TipSolution





pop_by_continent <- gapminder %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarize(pop_millions = sum(pop) / 1e6, .groups = "drop")

p_pop <- ggplot(pop_by_continent, aes(x = year, y = pop_millions)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population (millions)")

p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(continent))
p_pop + facet_wrap(vars(continent), scales = "free_y")










Fixed axes compare sizes: Asia grows from about 1,395 to 3,812 million, and Oceania (2 countries, 10.7 to 24.5 million) looks flat. Free axes compare shapes: Oceania more than doubles, like the others. Each is honest only if the reader notices the axes: with free y, say so in the caption, because panels of equal height no longer mean equal numbers.

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
section: D5 · Two facets at once: sex and species
text:
D5 · Two facets at once: sex and species
Prepares Guided Project task 3: panels by two columns, and the n of what is left out.

penguins %>%
  drop_na(sex, body_mass_g) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 200) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(sex), cols = vars(species)) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Penguins")








Talk. What can you compare across a row? Down a column? 11 penguins have no recorded sex (6 Adelie, 5 Gentoo) and are not in this plot: where would you tell the reader?






TipSolution





Across a row: the three species, for one sex (Gentoo are the heaviest). Down a column: females and males of one species (males are heavier in each). The shared axes make both comparisons fair. Say the 11 missing penguins in the caption or the text, with their n.

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D6 · Uncertainty clouds
Prepares Guided Project task 4 (A4, B4).
Goal. Is a difference between two groups large or small? Compared to what? Put each penguin next to the means of 200 resampled samples, on the same axis. (Session 2.)
Your turn. Compare Adelie and Chinstrap flipper lengths. The prepared code draws each species’ penguins again (with replacement, the same number), 200 times, and keeps each sample’s mean. Then make one panel per kind.

set.seed(3901)
flippers <- penguins %>%
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap")) %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
  select(species, flipper_length_mm)

means <- map(1:200, function(i) {
  flippers %>%
    group_by(species) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) %>%
    summarize(flipper_length_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

clouds <- bind_rows(
  flippers %>% mutate(kind = "Individual penguins"),
  means %>% mutate(kind = "Resampled means")
)


ggplot(clouds, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ ___) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper length (mm)")

Investigate. In which panel do the two clouds overlap? What does that say about two penguins, and about the two means?






TipSolution






ggplot(clouds, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ kind) +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper length (mm)")







clouds %>%
  group_by(kind, species) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean = mean(flipper_length_mm),
            lowest = min(flipper_length_mm),
            highest = max(flipper_length_mm), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  kind                species       n  mean lowest highest
  <chr>               <fct>     <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Individual penguins Adelie      151  190.   172     210 
2 Individual penguins Chinstrap    68  196.   178     212 
3 Resampled means     Adelie      200  190.   189.    191.
4 Resampled means     Chinstrap   200  196.   194.    198.


In the left panel the clouds overlap almost completely: Adelie flippers run from 172 to 210 mm, Chinstrap from 178 to 212 mm, so many Adelie penguins have longer flippers than many Chinstrap ones. In the right panel the 200 resampled means don’t overlap: Adelie’s from 188.7 to 191.3 mm, Chinstrap’s from 193.6 to 197.8 mm. The gap between the means, 5.9 mm (189.95 and 195.82), is small next to the spread of the penguins (sd 6.5 and 7.1 mm) but large next to how far each mean moves from sample to sample. Say which you compare: individuals or means. Chinstrap’s cloud of means is wider: 68 penguins, against Adelie’s 151.
In the Guided Project, make_clouds() does the resampling for you.




Watch the means settle
Draw 200 samples of 10, of 50, and of each species’ full size (with replacement), and plot each sample’s mean flipper length.

set.seed(3901)
flippers <- drop_na(penguins, flipper_length_mm)

cloud <- map_dfr(c(10, 50, NA), function(size) {
  map_dfr(1:200, function(i) {
    grouped <- group_by(flippers, species)
    drawn <- if (is.na(size)) {
      slice_sample(grouped, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)   # each species' n
    } else {
      slice_sample(grouped, n = size, replace = TRUE)
    }
    drawn %>%
      summarize(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm), .groups = "drop") %>%
      mutate(sample = if (is.na(size)) "All penguins" else
               paste(size, "penguins"))
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(sample = fct_inorder(sample))

ggplot(cloud, aes(x = mean_mm, y = species)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(vars(sample), ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean flipper length of one sample (mm)", y = NULL)







cloud %>%
  group_by(sample, species) %>%
  summarize(spread_sd = sd(mean_mm), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 9 × 3
  sample       species   spread_sd
  <fct>        <fct>         <dbl>
1 10 penguins  Adelie        2.10 
2 10 penguins  Chinstrap     2.14 
3 10 penguins  Gentoo        2.09 
4 50 penguins  Adelie        0.932
5 50 penguins  Chinstrap     0.932
6 50 penguins  Gentoo        0.908
7 All penguins Adelie        0.520
8 All penguins Chinstrap     0.824
9 All penguins Gentoo        0.612


The bigger the sample, the less its mean moves from one sample to the next. For Adelie, the spread (sd) of the 200 means is about 2.1 mm with 10 penguins, 0.93 mm with 50, and 0.52 mm with all 151. In one sentence, the central limit theorem: means of larger samples pile up in a narrower, bell-shaped cloud around the true mean, and the cloud’s width shrinks with the square root of the sample size. So “compared to what?” matters: a difference between two means is big or small compared to that width (the se), not to the spread of the penguins themselves (the sd).

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D7 · Color for every reader
Prepares Guided Project task 5 (A5, B5).
Goal. Colors every reader can tell apart, and never color alone. (Session 1.)
species_labels <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm, bill_length_mm) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(flipper_length_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm),
            bill_length_mm = max(bill_length_mm))

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_label(data = species_labels, aes(label = species)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)")
gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", color = "Continent")










What the numbers mean. We simulate how the colors look to readers with three types of color blindness, then measure how far apart the two closest colors are (a standard color difference, delta E). Bigger is easier to tell apart; 20 is our course’s line for clearly different. The red-green simulations come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one is an approximation. (In the Guided Project, color_check() makes this table for your plot, and simulate_plot() redraws your plot in the simulated colors.)



Smallest difference between any two colors.


view

5 continents

41.1

29.7

Talk. Which plot passes the course rule (at least 20 in all three rows)? What could carry the continents instead of color alone?






TipSolution





Three species pass (30.5, 41.1 and 29.7); five continents fail (17.5, 19.7 and 17.2): with more groups the colors have less room. The penguin plot also names each species on the plot, so color is never the only cue. For the continents: panels (facet_wrap(vars(continent)), D4), direct labels, or fewer groups, combined with care and said in the caption.



Where the numbers come from. The simulations use the model of Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009), at full severity. The red-green simulations come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one is an approximation.
Machado, G. M., Oliveira, M. M., & Fernandes, L. A. F. (2009). A physiologically-based model for simulation of color vision deficiency. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 15(6), 1291–1298. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.113

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
text:
D8 · Check a deck
Prepares Guided Project task 6 (your slides).
Goal. Check a finished deck against the minimum elements. (Session 2.)
Your turn. Open the penguins slides in the Example menu of your own site (or the course example). Find each element: title; question (naming the groups compared); data (source, what one row is, how many rows); figure; what it shows (a headline that states the finding); limitations; sources and AI use.
Investigate. Which elements share a slide? Which one is missing, and does your deck need it?






TipSolution





The question is the title (“Do penguin species differ in flipper length?”). The headline slide states the finding in its heading, with the figure under it. The last slide holds what it shows, the limitations (344 penguins, three islands, 2 without a flipper measurement) and the data source: elements can share a slide. There is no AI use line, because the example wasn’t made with AI; your deck needs one (“AI use: none.” counts).

title: Module 13 · Practice: scales and facets
section: D9 · More scale choices: size, gray fills, redundant cues
text:
D9 · More scale choices: size, gray fills, redundant cues
Prepares Guided Project task 5 (a second cue besides color) and task 2 (honest sizes).

Size: area or radius?
p_size <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDP per person (US$, log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", size = "Population")

p_size + scale_size_area(max_size = 12, labels = scales::comma)
p_size + scale_radius(range = c(1, 12), labels = scales::comma)










Readers judge circles by their area. With scale_size_area() area is proportional to population, so a country twice as large has twice the ink. With scale_radius() the radius is proportional, so the area grows with the square: big countries are exaggerated (a Lie Factor above 1).


Gray fills, no optical art

ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_grey(start = 0.25, end = 0.75) +
  labs(x = "Penguins", y = "Island", fill = "Species")








Hatching and stripes can shimmer on screen (Tufte’s “optical art”). Plain gray shades print well and never vibrate; keep them few, and far enough apart.


One redundant cue

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                     color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)",
       color = "Species", shape = "Species")








Mapping species to both color and shape is redundant on purpose: it helps a reader who can’t tell the colors apart, or who prints the page in gray. It helps most with few groups and few overlapping points; with many groups, shapes get hard to tell apart too, and panels work better.

Data: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). Bryan, J. (2025). gapminder: Data from Gapminder (R package version 1.0.1), from Gapminder (https://www.gapminder.org). Minard’s numbers: HistData::Minard.troops (Friendly, Dray, Li & Bellhouse, 2026, HistData, R package version 1.1.1), used in class. Color simulation: Machado, Oliveira & Fernandes (2009), in D7.

Explain your colors (in the report)

Your instructor reads it (counts under Choices)



What the numbers mean. color_check() simulates how your colors look to readers with three types of color blindness, then measures how far apart the two closest colors are (a standard color difference, delta E). Bigger is easier to tell apart; 20 is our course’s line for clearly different. The three rows are red-green (deuteranopia), red-green (protanopia) and blue-yellow (approximate). Below 20? Choose a column with fewer categories, group rare ones with care (keep small groups visible and say so), or use panels.
See it, not only the numbers. simulate_plot() redraws your plot in the same simulated colors. Your report shows your plot and the red-green (deuteranopia) version side by side, and the other two views below them.
The red-green simulations come from a validated model; the blue-yellow one is an approximation. Machado, G. M., Oliveira, M. M., & Fernandes, L. A. F. (2009). A physiologically-based model for simulation of color vision deficiency. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 15(6), 1291–1298. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2009.113

What reads what: the script reads data/fairness.csv and data/sports.csv. The report and the slides read the script’s chunks. Render writes docs/reports/gp13_report.html and docs/presentations/gp13_slides.html. After a push, GitHub Pages publishes docs/.


One script, two outputs
scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R   ← you edit the code here
        │ chunks read by name
        ├──► reports/gp13_report.qmd        → your report page
        └──► presentations/gp13_slides.qmd  → your slides page






ImportantEdit the code in the script. The report and the slides only read it.



Your words (findings, headlines, limits) live in the report and the slides.


Each chunk in the script starts with a label line such as ## ---- a1 ----. The report and the slides call the same chunks by name (with knitr::read_chunk()), so when you change a plot in the script and render, both pages show the new plot. Rendering the report doesn’t render the slides: render both before you push.






WarningCommon mistake



If you type code into a chunk in the report or the slides, it is ignored: on render, that chunk runs the script’s code instead. Your change doesn’t show on the page, and the checks don’t see it. A new code chunk you add does run, but only on that page, so your report, slides and script no longer match. Keep those chunks empty and fix the code in the script.




Words you’ll see

Script: a file of R code you run a few lines at a time (Ctrl/Cmd + Enter). Here, scripts/gp13_scales_facets.R holds all the code.
Chunk: a block of code. In the script, the lines from one label line to the next; in a .qmd file, a block that starts with ```{r}.
Chunk label: a chunk’s name. In the script it’s a line such as ## ---- a1 ----; the report and the slides find the code by that name.
Quarto: the program that turns a .qmd file into a web page or slides.
.qmd file: a Quarto document: your words plus code chunks. Here, reports/gp13_report.qmd and presentations/gp13_slides.qmd.
knitr: the R package that runs a .qmd file’s code chunks and puts their output into the document.
Render: the Render button. knitr runs the code chunks, then Quarto builds the page or the slides. (R Markdown called this Knit.) It renders only the file that is open.
Report: the web page built from gp13_report.qmd: code, output and your findings.
Slides: the deck built from gp13_slides.qmd (revealjs: slides that open in a web browser; the arrow keys move between them).
knitr::read_chunk(): the line near the top of the report and the slides that reads the script’s chunks, so a chunk named a1 there runs the script’s a1 code.
Output: what code produces: a plot, a table, a PASS or TO DO line. Render’s output is an HTML file in docs/.
Commit: saves a snapshot of the files you ticked, with a message, in your project’s history (Git tab).
Push: sends your commits to your repository on GitHub (with your token).
GitHub Pages: the GitHub service that publishes your repository’s docs/ folder as your website, a minute or two after a push.
URL: a web address. Your two pages’ URLs are the links you submit.



Ideas for your columns
Starting points; check them in the column list Section 0 prints for your own file (name, type, how many different values). Each dataset gets the same kind of hint: task 2 (a skewed column, or a share for percent labels), task 3 (panels: a group or a year), task 4 (two groups and a numeric column) and task 5 (a column with 2 to 4 categories, or how to make one). Small groups stay in your plots, with their n.
Fairness

Adult: task 2 capital_gain (most are 0: keep values above 0 with filter() and say how many); task 3 race; task 4 hours_per_week (or age) by sex; task 5 sex or income.

Credit Card: task 2 limit_bal; task 3 sex or marriage; task 4 age (or limit_bal) by sex; task 5 sex, or marriage (two small groups).

WNBA: task 2 a share of wins with percent labels; task 3 season_type (2 regular season, 3 playoffs: name them with if_else()); task 4 make a number first: each team’s share of wins in a season, at home and away (group_by() team, season and team_home_away, then summarize()), then the clouds by team_home_away; task 5 team_home_away.
NFL Draft Combine: task 2 a share picked in round 1; task 3 make a group from Round (empty = not drafted) with if_else(); task 4 forty for drafted and not drafted; task 5 that group.
Boston Marathon: task 2 a share finishing under a time you choose, from finish_net_minutes; task 3 gender or age_group (80+ has n = 5: keep it); task 4 finish_net_minutes by gender; task 5 gender. Never use name, bib_number or team.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Predict
Bill length and bill depth: when one goes up, does the other go up or down? Will the answer change once each species gets its own color? Write your prediction before running anything.






TipShow answer





Look at the two plots below. Without color, the whole cloud tends to go down: longer bills look shallower. With color, within each species the points go up. The overall trend mixes three groups that sit in different places. Mapping the group to color reveals it.

Investigate

What does one point stand for? What does the warning in the console say, and why?
Why map species to both color and shape?
You will set alpha = 0.4 below. Why is alpha set (outside aes()) and not mapped?

One penguin. Rows with a missing bill length or depth have no position, so geom_point() removes them and says so in the warning.
Two cues for the same column: the plot still reads in grayscale and for readers who do not see color differences (color is never the only cue).
Transparency here is not information about each penguin; it is one design choice for all points so overlaps show. One value for every mark is a setting.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Investigate

How many rows does penguin_means have? Why that number?
Run both plots below. Which geom follows the order of the rows, and which sorts by x first?


walk <- tibble(step = c(1, 3, 2), place = c(10, 30, 15))
ggplot(walk, aes(x = step, y = place)) + geom_line()







ggplot(walk, aes(x = step, y = place)) + geom_path()









The x axis shows values like 2007.5. Is that a problem with the data or with the axis?







TipShow answers






Nine: 3 species × 3 years, one row per combination.
geom_path() follows the row order (1, 3, 2); geom_line() sorts by x (1, 2, 3). Minard’s map is a path: the army’s route, in order.
The axis: ggplot2 chose breaks for a continuous number. Changing breaks is part of scales (Module 13).

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
In Part 1 you made your own repository on GitHub, turned on its website, and opened a working copy in Posit Cloud. Right now the copy only goes one way: from GitHub into Posit Cloud. In this tutorial you make it go both ways, so that the reports and slides you write in Posit Cloud reach GitHub and appear on your website. At the end, your home page shows your name at your own address.
You don’t need any experience with Git. Every step says what to click and what you should see. If something looks different, If something goes wrong lists the usual causes.











GitHub repository
Posit Cloud project




What it is
The shared copy. Public. Keeps the full history.
Your working copy. Where you write R and Quarto.


Your website
Shows what is in its docs/ folder
Changes here are invisible until you push


Direction
pull brings GitHub’s changes down to Posit Cloud
push sends your commits up to GitHub



The routine is always the same: edit → render → commit → push → check your site.










Word
Meaning




Git
The program that records versions of your files. It runs inside Posit Cloud; you click its buttons in the Git tab.


Commit
A saved snapshot of the files you chose, with a short message saying what changed. It stays in Posit Cloud until you push.


Stage
Tick a file’s box to include it in the next commit.


Push
Send your commits from Posit Cloud up to GitHub.


Pull
Bring commits from GitHub down into Posit Cloud (for example, a change you made on github.com).


Personal access token
A long secret code GitHub gives you to use instead of your password when you push. Treat it exactly like a password.


Render
Run Quarto to turn your .qmd files into the web pages in docs/.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
Task
Open your cis-3901-projects project in Posit Cloud (space CIS-3901-Fall2026) and keep this page open in another browser tab, next to a tab on GitHub. Do the steps in order; each takes 5 to 10 minutes.

Step 0. Check the packages (2 to 5 minutes)
Rendering the site needs the tidyverse and rmarkdown. In the Console, run:
needed <- c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown")
needed[!needed %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

If it prints character(0), everything is installed: go to Step A.
If it prints a package name, install what’s missing. This takes a few minutes; wait for the > prompt to come back.

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown"))


Step A. Tell Git who you are (5 minutes)
Every commit is signed with a name and an email. Your repository is public, so use GitHub’s private noreply email instead of your real one.

On GitHub: click your profile picture (top right) › Settings › Emails.
Tick Keep my email addresses private. GitHub then shows your noreply address, which looks like 12345678+your-username@users.noreply.github.com. Copy it.
In Posit Cloud, click the Terminal tab (next to Console). Type these two lines, one at a time, pressing Enter after each. Use your own name (a first name and last initial is fine) and the address you copied, both inside the quotes:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "12345678+your-username@users.noreply.github.com"

Check: type git config --global --list and press Enter. You should see your user.name and user.email.







TipGood to know



You do this once per Posit Cloud project. If you make another project from a Git repository later, repeat this step there.




Step B. Create your token (10 minutes)
GitHub doesn’t accept your password from Posit Cloud. It accepts a personal access token limited to one repository.

Open the token form: Create my CIS-3901 token. It opens GitHub’s form with the name, description, a 60-day expiration and the right permission already filled in. (Without the link: profile picture › Settings › Developer settings › Personal access tokens › Fine-grained tokens › Generate new token.)
Check or set these fields:

Token name: CIS-3901 Posit Cloud
Expiration: 60 days (past the Dec 4 presentations).
Repository access: choose Only select repositories, then pick cis-3901-projects. The link can’t fill this one in for you.
Permissions › Repository permissions › Contents: Read and write. (Metadata: Read-only is added automatically.) Leave everything else as it is.

Click Generate token. GitHub shows the token, starting with github_pat_, only once. Click the copy icon.
Keep it somewhere safe for the next 10 minutes: a password manager is best. If you lose it, you can always make a new one (see If something goes wrong).







WarningA token is a password



Never paste it into a file in your project, a commit message, a chat, an email, Blackboard or an AI tool.
Anyone with it can change your repository. If you think it leaked: GitHub › Settings › Developer settings › Fine-grained tokens › Delete, then create a new one.




Step C. Your first commit and push (10 minutes)

In the Files pane, open index.qmd. Near the top, replace Your Name with your name (again, first name and last initial is fine). Save the file (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on a Mac).
Click the Git tab (top-right pane). index.qmd appears with a blue M (modified).
Tick the Staged box next to index.qmd. If you also see a file ending in .Rproj with a yellow ?, tick it too: it’s your project’s settings file.
Click Commit. A Review Changes window opens. In Commit message, type Add my name to the home page, then click Commit. Read the small report, then click Close.
Click the green Push arrow (↑). Posit Cloud asks two questions:

Username: your GitHub username.
Password: paste your token (not your GitHub password). Nothing appears while you paste; that’s normal. Press Enter.

When the report ends with a line like main -> main, click Close.
On GitHub, reload your repository. Near the top you see your commit message and “now” or “1 minute ago”. Click index.qmd: your name is there.







NoteWhy your website hasn’t changed yet



Your site shows the docs/ folder, and docs/ still holds the old rendered page. Step D renders the site so docs/ has your name too.


Posit Cloud remembers your token for up to 12 hours, in memory only (never in a file). After that, or after the project restarts, it asks again: paste the token again.


Step D. Render and publish (10 minutes)

In the Terminal tab, type quarto render and press Enter. Quarto renders each page and reports Output created: docs/index.html at the end (about 1 minute). Or use the Build tab › Render Website.
In the Git tab you now see many changed files in docs/. Click Commit.
In the Review Changes window, click once in the file list, press Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on a Mac), then click Stage. Every box is ticked.
Message: Render site with my name. Click Commit, then Close, then Push (↑), then Close.
Wait 1 to 2 minutes, then open your site: https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/. Reload (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R). Your name is on the home page.



Step E. One habit: pull first (2 minutes)
If you ever change a file on github.com (for example, you fix a typo in README.md there), GitHub has a commit that Posit Cloud doesn’t. Bring it down before you start working: in the Git tab, click the blue Pull arrow (↓).






ImportantYour routine for every work session




Pull (↓).
Edit and save.
Render (quarto render).
Stage and Commit with a clear message.
Push (↑).
Check your site.

Commit small and often. Every commit is a point you can go back to.

section: Using GitHub Copilot as a helper (optional)
text:
Using GitHub Copilot as a helper (optional)
GitHub Copilot is GitHub’s AI assistant. Used well, it explains instead of doing: what an error message means, what a Git word means, what a line in a file does. You still click the buttons and make the decisions.
How to get it

Copilot Free comes with every GitHub account, with a monthly limit. Open https://github.com/copilot and start a chat.
Copilot Student (more use, free) requires GitHub Education verification: https://github.com/settings/education/benefits. Approval can take several days, and GitHub has paused new student sign-ups at times in 2026; Copilot Free is enough for this tutorial.
In Posit Cloud (code suggestions as you type): Tools › Global Options › Copilot, tick Enable GitHub Copilot, then sign in with the code it shows. You do this once per project.

Prompts that help

“I’m new to Git. Explain the difference between commit and push in two sentences.”
“I pushed from RStudio and got this message: [paste the message]. What does it mean, and what should I check?”
Open a file on GitHub and ask Copilot: “Explain what _quarto.yml controls in this repository.”







WarningRules




Never share your token with Copilot or any AI tool. Before you paste an error message, check it doesn’t contain a token or your email.
Check what Copilot says against this tutorial. If they disagree, follow the tutorial and ask in office hours.
In graded work, AI use follows that assignment’s AI level (see the AI Use Levels document) and must be logged as it says.

text:
If something goes wrong








What you see
Why
What to do




Authentication failed or Invalid username or token
You typed your GitHub password, or the token was cut off when you copied it.
Push again and paste the whole token (it starts with github_pat_). Still failing: make a new token (Regenerate).


403, Permission denied, or Write access to repository not granted
The token can’t write to this repository.
GitHub › Settings › Developer settings › Fine-grained tokens › your token › Edit: Repository access must include cis-3901-projects; Contents: Read and write. Save, then push again.


Please tell me who you are when you commit
Step A not done in this project.
Do Step A, then commit again.


GH007: Your push would publish a private email address
The commit used your real email while GitHub keeps it private.
Do Step A with the noreply address, then in the Terminal run git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit and push again.


Push rejected: fetch first or Updates were rejected
GitHub has a commit you don’t have (you edited on github.com).
Click Pull (↓), then Push (↑).


The token stopped working after weeks
It expired.
Fine-grained tokens › your token › Regenerate token, or create a new one as in Step B.


You lost the token
GitHub shows it only once.
Regenerate it, or delete it and create a new one.


Asked for username and token again
Normal: Posit Cloud forgets it after 12 hours or a restart.
Paste the token again.


Commit button does nothing, or nothing to commit
The file isn’t saved, or no box is ticked.
Save (the file name turns black), tick Staged, then Commit.


quarto render says there is no package called ...
A package is missing.
Do Step 0, then render again.


Site still shows Your Name
docs/ wasn’t rendered, staged or pushed; or the browser shows an old copy.
Repeat Step D; reload with Ctrl+Shift+R. On GitHub, the Actions tab shows pages build and deployment finishing.


Site shows 404
Pages is off or set to the wrong folder.
Settings › Pages: Deploy from a branch, main, /docs, Save. Check the address: your username and cis-3901-projects.



Still stuck? Copy the exact message (without any token), take a screenshot, and bring it to office hours or send it through Blackboard. Nothing you do here can break the course template, and GitHub keeps every commit, so mistakes can be undone.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Words you’ll use

Share: a part ÷ a total. It has no unit. Always say of what.
Rate: a share of a group that has an outcome: outcome count ÷ group size (e.g., a school’s graduation rate). This is question A.
Question B: of everyone with the outcome, what share is each group? Same counts, a different total.
sd = spread of the individuals; se = spread of the mean (or rate): how much it would move with another sample of the same size.
Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57): how many times a picture exaggerates a difference.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Steps
All steps happen in your cis-3901-projects project in Posit Cloud (course space CIS-3901-Fall2026), not in a new assignment. Keep this page open while you work.

Step 0 · One-time setting (1 minute)
Tools → Project Options → General: set Restore .RData into workspace at startup to No and Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Then Session → Restart R. (This stops old objects from coming back and hiding errors.)


Step 1 · Bring your two data files (5 minutes)
Your verified Fairness file (fairness.csv) and your Sports file (sports.csv) are in the data/ folder of your Module 11 Guided Project, guided_project_aes_geoms.

Open guided_project_aes_geoms. In the Files pane, open data/, tick only fairness.csv → More → Export → Download. Do the same for sports.csv. (One file at a time: ticking both downloads a zip.)
Open cis-3901-projects. In the Files pane:

go to data/tidy/ → Upload → fairness.csv;
go to data/sports/ → Upload → sports.csv.


Names matter: exactly data/tidy/fairness.csv and data/sports/sports.csv. If your browser renamed a download (for example fairness (1).csv), rename it in the Files pane (tick it → Rename). If you upload a file to the top folder or to data/ by mistake, the script moves it to the right place and tells you.
Your data files are published with your report. You push them to your public repository in step 5, so anyone can see them, as with your report.
Privacy: private people’s names must not be in your files or in your plots (for example, runners’ names in the Boston Marathon data). Professional athletes, teams and officials are public figures and are fine.


Step 2 · Add the starter files (2 minutes)
Download gp12_starter.zip from Blackboard. In cis-3901-projects, go to the top folder (project) → Upload → the zip. Posit Cloud unzips it and adds:

section: Ideas for your columns (check them with glimpse())
text:
Ideas for your columns (check them with glimpse())
Use these as starting points; check them with glimpse() in your own file. Every class dataset gets the same kind of hint. Small groups stay in your plots, with their n.
Fairness

Adult: group sex or race; outcome income == ">50K".
ACS Income: group sex or str_trunc(race, 30) (the full race labels are too long for a plot, and some groups are very small: one has n = 1, so a3_start must be below 1); outcome income > 50000.
Diabetes Hospital: group race or age (three bands); outcome readmit_30_days == 1.
Credit Card (fairness.csv = your clients file): group sex or education (one group has n = 2); outcome default_next_month == "yes".

Sports

NFL Draft Combine: group position; outcome Round %in% 1 (picked in round 1; Round is empty for players not drafted, and %in% counts them as FALSE); value forty.
WNBA game statistics: group team_home_away; outcome team_winner. The file has no score column, so use the days since the team’s previous game as the value: start with sports %>% arrange(game_date) %>% group_by(team_id, season) %>% mutate(...), with value = as.numeric(game_date - lag(game_date)) inside mutate(), then add %>% ungroup(). Home and away have the same count, so B3’s Lie Factor is 1.
Setka Cup table tennis: group sets played, factor(Sets_P1 + Sets_P2) (3, 4 or 5; factor() makes them groups, not a number line); outcome HomeWinner == 1; value points in game 1, P1_G1 + P2_G1.
Sumo: group the rank’s first letter, str_sub(Rank, 1, 1); outcome wins > losses; value weight_kg or height_cm.
WTA Grand Slam matches: group surface or round; outcome minutes > 120 (or a threshold you choose); value minutes. Some matches have no minutes: they show as NA in the legend of A1-style plots.
MMA fight decisions: group factor(rounds) (3, 5 or 12); outcome agreement == "Agree" (all three judges agree); value abs(judge1_margin). (Not result_type: Unanimous almost always means Agree, so its rates are close to 0% or 100%.)
MLB pitches: group player_name or pitch_type (includes NA and types with n = 2 or 5: they stay, with their n); outcome result == "S" (a strike); value release_speed.

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D1 · Count → share (question A)
Goal. Which island has the largest share of Adelie penguins? (Session 1, slides 10 and 17.)
Your turn. Make a group and an outcome, then plot the share of each group with the outcome, groups down the side.

d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = ___,                       # the islands
    has_outcome = ___                  # TRUE when the penguin is Adelie
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "___")

Investigate. What total does each bar divide by? Why can islands of different sizes now be compared?






TipSolution






d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = island,
    has_outcome = species == "Adelie"
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the island", y = NULL, fill = "Adelie")








Each bar divides by its own island’s total (Biscoe 168, Dream 124, Torgersen 52), so every bar runs from 0 to 1 and the unit “penguins” cancels. Torgersen is 100% Adelie; Dream about 45%; Biscoe about 26%.




D1+ · Read and discuss: counties or people? (no code to write)
The same numbers can be counted per county or per person. midwest (built into ggplot2) has one row per county in five Midwest states.
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "Counties")
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty, weight = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "People")










Talk. The left plot counts counties; the right counts people. Why do they look different? Which one answers “how many people live in poor counties?” (This is choosing the unit, the same idea as choosing the total. Source: ggplot2 book §5.2.)

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
section: D2 · A summary with its spread
text:
D2 · A summary with its spread
Goal. Show each species’ rate of heavy penguins (over 4000 g) with its standard error and its n. (Session 1, slides 13–16.)
Your turn. Finish the summary, then draw the rates with ±se.

d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = ___                           # the se of a rate
  )

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3)

Investigate. Whose range is widest? Look at its n and its rate.






TipSolution






d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )
d2_rates

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species       n  rate      se
  <chr>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Adelie      151 0.232 0.0343 
2 Chinstrap    68 0.221 0.0503 
3 Gentoo      123 0.992 0.00810

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Share heavier than 4000 g", y = NULL)








The se of a rate is sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n): it grows when n is small and when the rate is near 0.5. Chinstrap has the smallest n, so its range is wide; Gentoo’s rate is close to 1, so its range is narrow even with a similar n to Adelie.




D2b · A mean with its two spreads (Guided Project B2)

d2b <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    sd = sd(flipper_length_mm),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )
d2b

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  species       n  mean    sd    se
  <chr>     <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelie      151  190.  6.54 0.532
2 Chinstrap    68  196.  7.13 0.865
3 Gentoo      123  217.  6.48 0.585


Investigate. Chinstrap’s mean is about 5.9 mm above Adelie’s. Big compared to the se? Compared to the sd? (Session 2, slide 7.)






TipSolution





Compared to the se (under 1 mm), 5.9 mm is large: we are confident the means differ. Compared to the sd (about 6.5–7 mm), it is less than one sd: many individual Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have similar flippers. Say which comparison you mean.





D2+ · Optional: see the noise (resampling)
Redraw the penguins with replacement 200 times and compute each species’ rate again. The width of each cloud is the uncertainty the se describes. (map() and slice_sample() are new; read and run, no need to write them.)

# same redraws every time you run it
set.seed(3901)
resamples <- map(1:200, \(i) {
  penguins %>%
    drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) %>%
    group_by(species) %>%
    summarize(rate = mean(body_mass_g > 4000))
}) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "draw")

ggplot(resamples, aes(x = rate, y = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "Rate in each of 200 redraws", y = NULL)








Talk. Which species’ cloud is widest? Does that match D2’s ranges?

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D3 · Zoom or filter?
Goal. See what a zoomed axis does to bars, and compute its Lie Factor. (Session 2, slides 4–7.)
Your turn. Zoom the counts so the view starts at 40, then filter with the same limits.

d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + ___(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)   # zoom
d3_counts + ___(limits = c(40, 175))                 # filter

Investigate. Compute the Lie Factor of the zoomed plot for Biscoe (168) vs Torgersen (52).






TipSolution





d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)
d3_counts + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 175))











drawn_ratio <- (168 - 40) / (52 - 40)
data_ratio <- 168 / 52
drawn_ratio / data_ratio

[1] 3.301587


The zoom keeps all the data but cuts the bars at 40: Biscoe looks about 10.7 times longer than Torgersen, while the counts differ 3.2 times, a Lie Factor of about 3.3. The filter removes the bars, because every bar starts at 0, outside the limits. Bars start at 0; to look closer, use points and say so.




D3+ · Compared to what? A narrow time window
economics (built into ggplot2) has monthly US data from 1967 to 2015.
economics %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01"), date < as.Date("2008-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 2000–2007")
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 1967–2015")










Talk. What story does the left plot tell on its own? What does the full series add? Why divide by pop? (Tufte’s “compared to what?” and standardized units, 2001, p. 77.)






TipSolution





The 2000–2007 window shows a rise and a fall that look dramatic; the full series shows they are small next to the peaks of the early 1980s and 2009. Dividing by the population makes years comparable: the number unemployed grows partly because the population grows.

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D4 · Change the frame
Goal. Ask question B (of all Adelie, what share lives on each island?) and compare the frames. (Session 1, slide 17; Session 2, slides 9–11.)
Your turn. Keep the Adelie, count per island, and turn the counts into shares of all Adelie. Draw them sideways.

d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = ___)

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col()

Investigate. D1 said Torgersen is the “most Adelie” island. Does D4 agree?






TipSolution






d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
d4_shares

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  island        n share
  <chr>     <int> <dbl>
1 Biscoe       44 0.289
2 Dream        56 0.368
3 Torgersen    52 0.342

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of all Adelie", y = NULL)








No: of all 152 Adelie, Dream holds the largest share (about 37%), Torgersen 34%, Biscoe 29%. Question A (÷ island total) and question B (÷ Adelie total) answer different questions; say which one you mean.




D4+ · Bar or pie?
p_share <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = "all", fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of all penguins")
p_share
p_share + coord_polar(theta = "y")










Talk. Adelie (44%) or Gentoo (36%): which is easier to compare on the bar, and on the pie? Why? (Tufte, 2001, p. 77: don’t show more dimensions than the data have.)






TipSolution





On the bar, both are lengths on one scale from 0 to 1, easy to compare. On the pie, you compare angles and areas, which people judge less accurately, especially when slices are close. The data have one dimension (a share per species); the pie spreads it over angle and area: more work for the reader, and no new information. Prefer the bar.




Data: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). midwest and economics come with ggplot2 (Wickham, Navarro & Pedersen, ggplot2, 3rd ed.).
